title: Israel's IsraAID in Mozambique after Cyclone Idai: water, medicine and protection for more than 9,500 people

trailer.text: IsraAID, an international humanitarian aid organization based in Israel that was founded in 2001 and has worked in more than 60 countries, sent an emergency team to Mozambique after it was hit by Cyclone Idai.
The city of Beira, the fourth largest in Mozambique, took a direct hit and was almost entirely destroyed.
On March 20 the organization began sending a 10-person emergency team, and more people were sent the following week.
In cooperation with local authorities and other relief organizations, the Israelis distributed basic supplies, provided psychological first aid and helped restore access to safe drinking water.
The team's water, sanitation, hygiene, protection and medical programs reached more than 9,500 people.

glance.value: Yotam Polizer won the Bronfman Prize, a prize of 100 thousand dollars for a humanitarian activist under the age of 50, for his work and the work of the organization as a whole.

paragraphs.text: According to the Jerusalem Post, Cyclone Idai crossed Mozambique days after incessant rains.

According to the spokesperson of the UN's World Meteorological Organization, if the death-toll estimates were borne out, Idai would be one of the worst weather-related disasters ever to strike the southern hemisphere.
The city of Beira, the fourth largest in Mozambique, took a direct hit.
It was almost entirely destroyed and almost completely cut off by storm surges.
An IsraAID spokesperson said that in the city the roofs of most buildings, including the hospital, were damaged, and many trees had fallen.
According to him, outside the city the situation was worse, and large areas were still under water and inaccessible by land.
UNICEF spokesperson Christophe Boulierac said that thousands were fighting for their lives sitting on rooftops, in trees and in other elevated places, among them many families and children.
Mozambique's President Filipe Nyusi said that the death toll could surpass 1,000.
UN Secretary-General Guterres expressed sorrow over the loss of life, the destruction and the displacement.
According to the report, IsraAID announced on Wednesday that it planned to send a team to Mozambique.
The organization planned to distribute relief supplies, provide psychological first aid and restore access to safe drinking water.
According to the organization's spokesperson, the mental health team would support affected communities, and the water team would install filtration systems and distribute hygiene kits.
On March 20 IsraAID began sending a 10-person emergency team, and more people were sent the following week.
According to Behold Israel, the organization acted as a first responder and sent aid and a psychological support team immediately after the cyclone.
It was not alone. The NATAN organization sent a medical team from Israel to Mozambique on March 26, in partnership with the JDC and the Jewish community of Mozambique.
The CEO of JDC said that aiding survivors and beginning the healing process are crucial on a long road to recovery.
In cooperation with local authorities and other relief organizations, the Israelis distributed basic supplies, provided psychological first aid and helped restore access to safe drinking water.
IsraAID's water engineer purified the drinking water of displaced families using the Israeli NUF filtration system.
The organization distributed household water-filtration systems to hundreds of families whose only water source is a shallow pool of water.
After an initial needs assessment, IsraAID sent a medical team of volunteer doctors and nurses from Sheba Medical Center.
The team arrived on the evening of March 26.
The NATAN team assisted a woman in labor immediately after she was transferred by helicopter to the Nhamatanda District.

stations.title: Families in shelter, children without school

paragraphs.text: On March 25 IsraAID met families who had lost their homes and were staying in a temporary shelter at the Samora Machel high school, the city's biggest.
Naama Gorodischer, head of IsraAID's mission in Mozambique, said that the school's principal dedicated all of her time to the families' well-being until they were moved to a new camp.
More than 143 thousand children were unable to attend school.
In partnership with the local Ministry of Education, IsraAID's team trained teachers and educational psychologists to prepare for the return to school.
The Red Cross and Red Crescent warned that survivors face “a ticking bomb” of disease.
IsraAID announced that it was sending Prof. Eli Schwartz, an infectious disease specialist, to assist with the over 1,000 reported cases of cholera.
Following cholera cases in Beira, Prof. Schwartz joined the local Cholera Task Force.
IsraAID's emergency team worked in Mozambique from Idai onward, providing water, sanitation, hygiene, protection and medical programs to more than 9,500 people.
Yotam Polizer, co-CEO of IsraAID, said that the team met with First Lady Isaura Nyusi, who will be a close partner in the mission, and that the organization will work there for the long term.
According to him, the organization would work there for the long term.
Then another cyclone came. Kenneth hit northern Mozambique on April 25 and killed at least 38 people, and IsraAID prepared to respond to it as well.
Polizer said that Mozambique had never been hit by two storms of this magnitude in the same season.
According to him, the team continued to work in Sofala province in the center of the country, including Buzi district, which were still in need of urgent assistance.
The organization states that it remains committed to communities even after the crisis is gone from the headlines.

stations.title: The organization and the people behind it

paragraphs.text: IsraAID was founded as an umbrella organization of Jewish and Israeli rescue, medical and aid bodies.
According to the article, the idea of establishing IsraAID emerged with Zahavi and others as its founders, and Zahavi ran the organization for 16 years, until he decided to leave in 2016.

Yotam Polizer was IsraAID's second employee, after founder Shachar Zahavi; according to an article from the time of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the organization then had 320 employees in 14 countries.
In 2018 IsraAID's emergency teams reached 26,300 people worldwide.
The organization had earlier also responded to disasters such as hurricanes in the United States and wildfires in California.
Polizer won the Bronfman Prize, a prize of 100 thousand dollars for a humanitarian activist under the age of 50, for his work and the work of the organization.
Charles Bronfman said that the organization is an entrepreneurial philanthropy and not a government body, and that it is usually the first to arrive in crisis areas.
